 November 20, 2026 2027 Minimum Wage Updates: What Employers Need to Know
 Advisory 
 Human Capital Management 
 Table of Contents Get in Touch 
 Share 
 A new year brings a new round of minimum wage increases. Many states will raise their minimum wage in 2027, most on January 1. Some increases are small inflation adjustments. Others are larger, scheduled jumps that may have a more significant effect on payroll budgets.
 For employers with hourly workers, these changes affect more than pay rates. They can affect budgets, pay equity, overtime, and compliance across every location where you have employees. Here’s what’s changing in 2027 and how to get your payroll ready.
 2027 State Minimum Wage Increases at a Glance
 Below are some of the key minimum wage changes confirmed for the year ahead, according to state labor department releases.

 This is not an exhaustive list — consult your state or local labor department for final numbers, effective dates, and tipped wage minimums. Minimum wage increases may differ for seasonal and small employers with fewer than six employees. 
 Key Highlights for 2027
 Highest state minimums: Washington ($17.73), Connecticut ($17.48), California ($17.40), and Rhode Island ($17.00) will have the highest minimum wages in 2027.
 Most significant jumps: Michigan will see the largest increase, rising $1.27 to $15.00. Alaska and Rhode Island will each go up $1.00, and Virginia will rise $0.98.
 The $15 mark keeps spreading: Michigan and Alaska will reach $15.00, joining the many states already at or above that level.
 Not every change starts January 1: Alaska’s increase takes effect July 1, 2027, so employers in that state will need a midyear payroll update. Other states and localities may also announce midyear minimum wage adjustments, so it’s important to watch for updates throughout the year.
 New York holds steady, for now: New York’s standard minimum wage will stay at $17.00 in New York City, Long Island, and Westchester County and $16.00 in the rest of the state on Jan. 1, 2027, due to an economic “off-ramp” being triggered in state law. Home care aides will still see an increase to $20.00 downstate and $19.00 elsewhere. Governor Hochul has proposed a change that could raise rates to $17.60 and $16.55 on March 1, 2027, if the legislature approves it.
 Steady, smaller increases: Most other states will raise minimum wage by about $0.25 to $0.60 per hour, likely due to automatic inflation adjustments.
 What 2027 Minimum Wage Updates Signal on a Broader Scale
 Inflation Indexing Is Becoming the Norm
 More states now build automatic inflation adjustments into their minimum wage laws, often tied to the Consumer Price Index or a similar measure. That means smaller, predictable increases each year instead of waiting for new legislation, and employers should plan for annual raises as a regular part of budgeting.
 The Pace of Increases Varies From State to State
 Many 2027 increases are modest inflation adjustments. However, states following a scheduled path to a higher wage, like Michigan, Alaska, and Rhode Island, are making bigger jumps. Employers with workers in several states should expect different rates, dates, and rules in each location.
 Wage Compression May Affect Internal Pay Equity
 When entry-level pay rises, the gap between new hires and more experienced employees can shrink. Employers should review pay bands, merit increases, and internal equity to avoid pay compression as the lowest wage levels move up.
 Looking Ahead: How Employers Can Prepare Payroll for 2027
 As minimum wage rates rise year over year, employers without appropriate systems in place may face mounting administrative and compliance pressure. Managing different rates across states, localities, and worker classifications can quickly become overwhelming.
 Before the new year, consider these steps:
 Confirm rates by location. Check state, county, and city rates for every location where you have employees, including remote workers.
 Update payroll systems before the effective date. Make sure new rates are in place for the first pay period they apply to, including midyear changes like Alaska’s July 1 increase.
 Review tipped and exempt employees. Minimum wage changes can affect tipped wage credits and, in some states, the salary threshold for exempt employees.
 Check for pay compression. Look at how increases affect pay gaps between new and longer-tenured employees.
 Update required postings. Replace workplace posters and employee notices with current versions.
 Budget for the full cost. Include payroll taxes, overtime, and other wage-based costs in your 2027 planning.
 Now is the time to modernize payroll operations. Outdated systems or manual processes can lead to costly compliance gaps and wage calculation errors. Investing in automation isn’t just about keeping up — it’s about staying ahead.
 Discover how CBIZ can help your organization optimize payroll processes now, so you can enter 2027 ready to thrive.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 When do most 2027 minimum wage increases take effect? 
 Most state increases take effect Jan. 1, 2027. Some, like Alaska’s, take effect later in the year, so check the effective date for each state where you have employees.
 Which minimum wage applies if city, state, and federal rates differ? 
 In general, employers must pay the highest rate that applies to the employee, whether that’s the federal, state, or local minimum wage.
 How can employers stay on top of yearly minimum wage changes? 
 Automated payroll technology and a trusted payroll partner can help track rate changes by location, update pay rates on time, and reduce the risk of costly errors.
